C-ADD-AMBIENT-MUSIC.Summary: Add a second audio channel — looping ambient music — beside the interface sounds, and move the audio control out of the hub into the shared header where a global setting belongs.
C-ADD-AMBIENT-MUSIC.Problem: The app gained interface sound in C-ADD-UI-SOUNDS, but it is silent between interactions, and the single sound switch sits in the hub's "Services" row: it scrolls away with the content and it is not the place a global preference belongs. Music is not a bigger version of an interface blip and cannot ride the same channel: it loops instead of firing once, it must stop when the app is not in front of the user, it needs its own volume (a menu bed sits far below a click), its own stored preference, and it must not be throttled by the 40 ms UI debounce. GT Sport's menus had exactly this shape — separate channels with separate volumes — which is also why the control belongs in the header rather than in a content block.

Goals.Goal: Loop ambient music in the background, rotating through the shipped tracks, so a long session does not repeat one two-minute loop forever.
Keep it a separate service with its own player seam, its own preference key and its own volume, so the interface-sound policy stays untouched.
Stop the music when the app is not foregrounded and bring it back when it is, because a companion app must not play to an empty room.
Ease the volume in and out instead of cutting, so starting and stopping does not click against the game's own audio.
Move the audio control into the shared header next to the clock, as one icon that opens a menu with two switches — interface sounds and ambient music — each reflecting its own stored state.
Delete the hub's own switch, so there is exactly one place to control audio.

Constraints.Constraint: Assets must be redistributable and their provenance recorded. Two tracks come from Open Lo-Fi, whose manifest and README declare CC0-1.0 ("without asking permission or giving credit"); game-ripped GT music remains out of bounds.
Keep the bundle honest: two tracks, about 8 MB together. No download at runtime, no streaming.
Music must never play in tests: the player is injected and a disabled service makes no call, as with the interface sounds.
The header is also the phone's bottom navigation bar, so the control must fit the existing row at both widths without disturbing the tabs, the central button or the clock.
Leave the interface-sound behaviour exactly as shipped: same sounds, same 40 ms debounce, same volume, same toggle semantics. This change adds a channel; it does not revise the old one.
The service lifecycle hook must be registered and removed cleanly, so no observer leaks when the scope is torn down.

NonGoals.NonGoal: No volume sliders: both channels stay on/off with fixed, deliberately low levels. A mixer is a separate design.
No track picker, no playlists, no per-screen music cues, no crossfade between tracks.
No music in the telemetry dashboard's own code, and no change to the telemetry or profile features.
The empty `lib/services/settings_service.dart` is still not resurrected.

AcceptanceCriteria.Criterion: assets/music/ holds the two tracks and a provenance note naming Open Lo-Fi, the CC0-1.0 license and the release URL, and pubspec registers the folder.

lib/services/music_player.dart defines the playback seam — start a looping track, set volume, stop, dispose — with the audioplayers implementation behind it and the audioplayers import appearing in no other service file.
lib/services/music_service.dart extends ChangeNotifier, exposes enabled, volume, load, setEnabled and dispose, persists to a ui_music_enabled key, and advances to the next track when one finishes.
The service observes the app lifecycle and pauses playback when the state is not resumed, resuming only if music is enabled.
AppScope registers the music service in dependency order.
AdaptiveNavBar carries one audio control that opens a menu with two switches, each reading and writing its own service, and the control's icon reflects whether any channel is on.
lib/pages/home_page.dart no longer contains the sound switch.

test/music_service_test.dart proves with a fake player that a disabled service never starts playback, that enabling starts it, that disabling stops it, and that finishing a track moves to the next one.
The whole suite stays green and flutter analyze reports no new issues on the pinned SDK.

VerificationIntent.ExpectedEvidence: The analyzer reports no new issues, the whole suite passes, and the new unit test proves the four behaviours above. Whether the music is actually audible, loops without a gap, and ducks out when the app loses focus can only be confirmed by running the app: the same instrumented-run technique used for the interface sounds (temporary logging inside the player's error-swallowing blocks, then reverted) is the intended evidence path, followed by listening on macOS.

Assumptions.Assumption: Open Lo-Fi's CC0 dedication holds: the author states the tracks were generated with Suno v5 and donated to the public domain, and the manifest records license CC0-1.0.
Two tracks are enough for rotation in this version; more can be added by dropping files into assets/music/ once the user listens and chooses.
Music is on by default at 0.25 because the app's stated character is a Gran Turismo companion, and the header control is always visible.
MP3 is acceptable on every platform this app targets; the interface sounds already proved asset loading works on macOS with OGG.
